chunks: "I'd start by asking what x is and what it has to do: the specs, the hazardous parts like high voltage or high current, and whether this is a one-off prototype or a production run.
Then I'd redraw the block diagram and test it in layers. First, no power: visual inspection, rail-to-ground resistance, and a polarity check.
Second, power-up with a current limit, bringing up one rail at a time if I can split them, checking voltage, ripple, sequencing and reset.
Third, each block on its own: for example the clock, then the communication to each chip, then the sensor or driver outputs against known inputs.
Fourth, the whole system doing its job against the spec, with numbers: accuracy, bandwidth, efficiency, whatever matters.
Fifth, stress and corners: supply min and max, temperature, load steps, and fault injection like a short on an output.
I'd define pass and fail numbers up front, use the right instruments, and log results. If there are many boards, I'd add test points and a fixture so it can be automated.
For x specifically, I'd adapt: for a power stage, efficiency and load transients; for a sensor board, calibration against a reference; for RF, a spectrum analyser or VNA."
